description: Cross-product Capability Coverage Guard. Every capability carries one of CURRENT/PARTIAL/PLANNED/BLOCKED/OUT_OF_SCOPE. CURRENT requires real implementation AND tests. Authored during Sprint 19 and extended each sprint since (gem/gem_visual: Sprint 21; arrangement: Sprint 22; family: Sprint 24) and validated by backend/tests/test_capability_coverage.py.

capabilities.note: geometry/setting + prong.py; 4/6 prongs; RADIAL + OUTLINE_CARDINAL placement.
geometry/setting + bezel.py; outline-offset wall; round/oval proven.

setting/channel.py; two parallel walls with the stones between them, running along a stated axis, with optional end caps. Extents default to the stone's own measured box. The stones are the Stone Arrangement Engine's: this family builds the walls and records which instances they hold, never where those instances are.

setting/flush.py; a solid collar offset from the stone's girdle outline with the stone's own solid cut out of it. Reuses the bezel's verified offset pipeline and the existing REFERENCE_SEAT relief, so the stone is a cutting tool and never becomes production metal. Relief is a PRECONDITION, not an option: JM-SETTING-010 reports a flush setting without it and the generator refuses.
setting/bar.py; transverse bars across a run, one component carrying every bar with each bar's own offset in its metadata. Spacing and length default to the stone's own measured extents.

setting/tension.py; two opposing supports with the stone between them, each reaching inward past its edge so the seat relief leaves a real groove. PARTIAL with COMPLETE geometry: a tension setting's whole function is structural, none of that behaviour is modelled (no force, no spring-back, no retention claim), and professional review is REQUIRED before the geometry means anything functional.

Deliberately NOT a setting family and will stay that way: repeated small-stone retention is setting/retention.py's builders driven by a pave field, and a second route to it would be a duplicate retention engine. The real capability is recorded under the pave domain.

Deriving a girdle outline by projecting imported geometry is not implemented; imported stones report no outline rather than a fabricated one, which is why their setting compatibility is UNSUPPORTED.

Cardinal, tip, cleft, lobe, wide/narrow-end and corner anchors are derived from the real outline. They are geometric facts, never prong positions.

gem/registry.py; 40 entries across minerals, organics, simulants and composites, plus 'custom' and 'unknown'. An internal taxonomy, not a gemological database; every entry is NOT_REVIEWED.
domain/schema.py::StoneSpec.gem; type/instance split — the registry says what a ruby is, the identity says what THIS ruby is.
NATURAL/SYNTHETIC/SIMULANT/COMPOSITE/UNKNOWN, checked against each entry's applicableOrigins by JM-GEM-002. Independent of treatment.
14 treatment types with PRESENT/NOT_PRESENT/SUSPECTED/UNKNOWN status and a disclosure source. Declaration only: no safety, durability or setting rule is derived from it.
gemId 'custom' with a required customName — the escape hatch for a material with no registry entry.
gemId 'unknown' and the resolution fallback. A legacy design with no gem normalizes here, never to diamond.
designer/gem_language.py; English and Italian names, origins and treatments, derived from the live registry. Cut/species terms (emerald, pearl) are reported ambiguous rather than resolved.
JewelMind makes no certification claim and stores no lab report as evidence. A treatment or origin field records what someone DECLARED.
No hardness, durability, heat-sensitivity or setting-suitability rule exists. Each requires professional evidence this project does not have, so none is implemented rather than guessed.
The escape hatch for sourced gem data. No external source is integrated; provenance SOURCED exists in the vocabulary and is used by no entry yet.
gem/models.py::StoneInstance carries a role and its own gem, but no generator builds more than one stone, so the arrangement half is PLANNED.
gem/visual.py; 20 profiles mirrored in frontend/src/vision/gemMaterials.ts. Every value is a RENDERING parameter, never an optical measurement.
vision/materials.ts::resolveComponentMaterial takes the gem's profile; an unrecognized profile renders the neutral fallback, not a diamond look.
stone.gem.visualProfileId; lets a pale sapphire look pale while still being a sapphire. Presentation only — it never changes identity.
No measured refractive index, dispersion or absorption spectrum. The renderer's ior/dispersion values are chosen for plausibility on screen.
arrangement/models.py::StoneInstanceDef; stable id, stone reference, gem reference, role, placement and a closed set of overrides. An occurrence references what a stone IS rather than restating it.
arrangement.instances/groups/patterns/relations in JDL; optional and nullable, so a pre-Sprint-22 document is a single-stone design and behaves exactly as before.
arrangement/resolve.py; one pass, closed-form pattern expansion, frame composition, canonical ordering. No solver, no iteration, no random ids.
arrangement/normalize.py; separate from definitionHash and geometryHash. Reordering instances cannot change it; the resolver version participates.
JM-ARRANGE-001..006 in validation/engine.py::_arrangement_rules. Structural and referential only — no spacing, proportion or density rule exists, and overlap is a geometric question for Inspection.
arrangement/compile.py, surfaced on GeneratedModel.arrangement_result. Reports each instance's generation status; NOT_GENERATED always carries a reason and GENERATED always names its component.

Primary instance keeps stone_reference exactly; an additional instance is stone_reference.<instanceId>, classified as a stone reference by geometry/roles.py rather than falling through to production_metal.

Sprint 24: every resolved instance naming the primary stone builds a REAL stone solid, named stone_reference.<instanceId>, classified as a stone reference and inspected as one. STILL PARTIAL because a SETTING is generated only for the primary instance — no accent-setting strategy exists, and inventing one would mean inventing setter geometry. See docs/bible/26-multi-stone-families/execution-boundary.md.

Sprint 24: scale and orientationDeg reach geometry. Scale is applied about the stone's own centre (scaling about the global origin would drop a stone sitting above the band), and orientation spins the stone about its own axis rather than swinging it around the design axis.
Five relation kinds are representable, reference-checked and preserved. They are DECLARATIONS: nothing moves an instance to satisfy one.
Placement relative to another INSTANCE needs a dependency order, and a cyclic reference has no determinate resolution. Group-relative placement is CURRENT.
Explicitly out of scope: a solver's output depends on iteration order and starting values, which this layer's determinism guarantee forbids.
Members along an arbitrary curve. Needs curve evaluation, which belongs to the geometry core, not to a declarative arrangement.
Tilt and roll. Deliberately not representable: a rotation no builder can execute would be a silently ignored field.

Sprint 24: multi-stone geometry exists, so Geometry Inspection reports pairwise intersections between stone components as geometric facts. PARTIAL because no rule INTERPRETS them: whether an overlap is acceptable is a professional question, and no spacing threshold is invented.
Minimum spacing, accent-to-centre proportion, pave density. Each needs sourced professional evidence this project does not have.
stoneRef resolves only 'primary' today because JDL carries one stone; any other value is reported unresolved (JM-ARRANGE-003) rather than silently treated as the primary one.
setting/prong_styles.py; ROUND (the preserved pre-Sprint-23 cylinder), TAPERED, CLAW and V, each a real solid from a registered builder. Notch and taper parameters are software construction values.

setting/head.py; BASKET (preserved byte-identically), PEG_HEAD, MARTINI and TULIP, each one connected solid. Head construction is now category-neutral; geometry/components/basket.py is a thin re-export.

positionSource='EXPLICIT' takes positions verbatim — the escape hatch for a layout no strategy derives. Never mixed with derived positions, because a half-overridden layout has no determinate meaning.
Named subsets carrying a per-prong style override, so a mixed layout (V prongs at a tip, round elsewhere) needs no second setting.

SettingGeometryResult.stoneInstanceAssignments maps each generated component to the stone instance IDs it serves, by ID rather than by inferred position. The Setting System carries the references and never resolves them, so it stays free of the arrangement layer.

PRONG_SHARED (Sprint 27): a prong serving two or more stones is expressed through EXPLICIT positions carrying servesStoneInstanceIds, the prongs are real solids, and the assignment is reported per component. PARTIAL because the shared POSITION is stated by the document rather than derived from the two stones' own geometry, so whether a shared prong reaches both stones it names is a geometric fact for inspection rather than a guarantee. No interface authors explicit positions yet.
Interwoven curved rails need a swept solid along a 3D spline, which the current pipeline cannot build verifiably. No builder exists, and TRELLIS is not a HeadArchitecture enum member.
A rail joins two or more heads, so it requires multi-head geometry. One setting builds one head today.
Placing prongs at a stone's own anchors (tip, cleft, corners). The anchors exist in Stone v2; no strategy consumes them, so OUTLINE_CARDINAL remains the non-round default.

A centre with two flanking stones. Compiles to a centre instance plus a MIRROR pattern when symmetric, or two explicit side instances when not. Real stone geometry for all three; only the primary stone receives a setting.

Two stones as a deliberate pair, straddling the design axis along a settable angle. Symmetric compiles to a mirror, which also flips a chiral stone's own orientation. Real stone geometry for both; only the primary stone receives a setting.

Stones grouped around an optional centre. Not necessarily circular (radiusYMm makes it elliptical) and not necessarily centred. Real stone geometry for every member; only the primary stone receives a setting.
The general centre-plus-accents family, for designs that are neither a strict three-stone nor a cluster. Real stone geometry for every member; only the primary stone receives a setting.
family/compile.py turns family semantics into arrangement primitives, so the Stone Arrangement Engine remains the sole placement authority. A registry, not a branch chain.

family/effective.py is the one place a family and an explicit arrangement meet. Declaring both is refused (JM-FAMILY-001) rather than merged: two authorities over one set of placements has no determinate resolution.

JM-FAMILY-001..005. Structural and referential only: one authority, valid roles, correct cardinality, resolvable references, and an honest report of what a compiled family does not get. No proportion, spacing or settability rule exists.
Members may carry different gem identities, scales and orientations, each REFERENCING the authoritative Gem and Stone systems rather than restating them.
A member's settingRef is carried and reported, but only the primary stone receives a setting. An accent-setting strategy does not exist.
A single head spanning several stones (a three-stone gallery, a cluster basket) needs multi-stone head geometry; Sprint 23 builds one head per setting.
Centre-to-accent proportion, minimum spacing, or whether a cluster is settable. Each needs sourced professional evidence this project does not have, so none exists.
halo, pave, eternity, bypass and channel_row are named with real reasons in family/capability.py::RESERVED_FAMILY_TYPES and have no compiler. A halo is already expressible as CENTER_WITH_ACCENTS.

geometry/stone/instance.py applies each resolved instance's own transform, scale and orientation to the built stone. An instance at the origin with no scale or rotation returns the builder's own shape object, so single-stone geometry is provably untouched.

Geometry Inspection derives its stone set from the role map, requires every stone component, and evaluates stone/metal separation across all of them. A stone-to-stone overlap is reported as a geometric fact, not as a separation failure.

One ring of stones around a centre, level with it. Every stone is an individually identifiable instance with real placed, scaled and oriented geometry. No metal holds them: only the primary stone receives a setting.

Two concentric rings, each with its own count, radius, start angle and scale — which is why a halo is not a CENTER_WITH_ACCENTS family, whose single accent parameter set cannot carry two rings. Real stone geometry for every stone in both rings; no halo metal.

One ring below the centre stone's girdle plane, which is what 'hidden' means structurally. The vertical offset reaches the solid through the arrangement's own transform, so the stones are genuinely lower — verified by measuring the built geometry's bounding box, not by trusting the field. No halo metal.

A halo composes onto a compiled family rather than replacing it, so centre + halo, centre + accents + halo, and three-stone + halo are one design each. The centre is resolved by id against the real compiled instances; an unresolvable centre is refused, never re-anchored. Halo stones get geometry; halo metal does not exist.
A halo composes onto an explicit arrangement the same way it composes onto a family, so a hand-placed multi-stone centre can carry one. Same stone-geometry and metal boundary.

centerMemberId=null anchors the halo on the design origin, which encircles a multi-stone centre (a toi-et-moi pair, a cluster) rather than one of its stones. What does NOT exist is a halo whose radius follows the combined outline of that centre: the ring is a circle or an ellipse, and no group-outline offset capability exists to make it hug an arbitrary group.

radiusYMm gives a second semi-axis, so a halo around an oval or marquise centre is an ellipse rather than a circle. A geometric parameter, not a claim that the result suits any particular centre stone.
sweepDeg under 360 lays a ring on an arc, with both endpoints included — the same closed-form distinction the arrangement resolver applies to a RADIAL pattern, from the same shared function.
A ring may carry its own GemIdentity and an individual stone may override it, resolved through the real Sprint 21 registry. Semantic only, exactly as for a single stone: it never affects geometry.

A ring's `members` list overrides individual stones' scale, orientation, gem and placement. Members are matched to positions by sorted id, never by array order, so reordering the list cannot move a stone. It reuses the family's own FamilyMember model rather than declaring a parallel one.

A halo stone's `stoneRef` may name a stone specification other than 'primary', and that reference is preserved and reported. It does not resolve, because JDL carries exactly one `stone` — so such a stone produces no geometry and says so (JM-HALO-004). A compass halo alternating shapes therefore cannot be built yet.

The metal that holds a halo — a shared bezel rail, a row of shared prongs, cut-down bead setting — does not exist. A ring's `settingRef` is carried and reported, and only the primary stone receives a setting. Sprint 23 built the contract a future strategy will use (explicit prong positions carrying servesStoneInstanceIds); SETTING-GOV requires an RFC before a halo setting family is added, and this sprint did not bypass it.
A halo whose stones follow the centre stone's own girdle outline (a cushion or emerald halo) needs an outline-offset walk that does not exist. An ellipse is offered and is honestly an ellipse.

Designer proposes flat scalar JDL paths only; neither `family` nor `halo` is in its allow-list, because a provider proposing a nested structure could not be diffed field by field or shown with real provenance. Adding halo alone would advertise a capability families do not have.

Minimum halo stone spacing, a centre-to-halo proportion, a settable radius, or whether a hidden halo clears the centre's pavilion. Each needs sourced professional evidence this project does not have, so none exists. Whether two placed stones overlap is a GEOMETRIC fact for Geometry Inspection.

A halo compiles into arrangement primitives and is COMPOSED onto whatever placement the design declares, at the single resolution point family/effective.py::effective_arrangement(). There is no second placement engine: the ring's angular sequence comes from arrangement/radial.py, the same function the resolver uses for a RADIAL pattern.
A named centerMemberId is resolved by id against the real compiled instances and refused if absent (JM-HALO-001), never silently re-anchored. centerMemberId=null anchors on the design origin.

JM-HALO-001..005: the centre resolves, the halo composes through the real compiler, the family/halo combination is supported, references resolve, and the metal-coverage limitation is reported. All structural; no professional threshold exists.
Reserved names with real reasons and no compiler: compass_halo, cushion_halo, floral_halo, pave_halo, triple_halo. Each is refused by the model rather than substituted with a SINGLE halo.
Surface population: an angular span and a row count filled at a stated pitch, so the designer gives the area and the density and the stone count follows. Real stone solids and real retention metal.

A stated retention topology: explicit rows and columns with explicit spacings, so the designer gives the structure and the area follows. The inverse specification of a PAVE, sharing its lattice, surface and retention primitives.

The shank's outer surface, cylindrical about the finger axis — the classic shank pavé. Executable because Sprint 26 gave the arrangement a real axis tilt, so each stone follows the surface normal instead of standing upright through the metal. Retention beads fuse into the band and a recess is cut out of it.

The horizontal plane at the top of the head. Planar, so no tilt is needed. The field is bounded away from the centre stone by the inner radius the Ring adapter reports, so a gallery pavé cannot land on top of the stone it surrounds.

The plane a declared halo's rings sit in, resolved from the real halo definition. PARTIAL because it requires a halo: a design without one is refused rather than given a substituted plane, and the pavé does not follow a hidden halo's own vertical offset — it sits in the plane the halo's inner ring defines.
Rows and columns aligned. Every row starts at the same angular position.
Alternate rows shifted by half the column pitch — the fixed 0.5 case of ROW_OFFSET, kept separate because a half shift is the case a designer names.
Every successive row shifted by a declared fraction of the column pitch, so a diagonal lattice is a parameter rather than a new pattern.

Stones distributed about the host surface's own axis. On a full 360-degree planar sweep the angular sequence comes from `arrangement/radial.py` — the same function the resolver uses for a RADIAL pattern — so a pavé ring and a hand-written one place their stones identically.

The document states each placement, carrying an arrangement `InstanceTransform` verbatim. The escape hatch for a field no lattice derives; refused rather than silently replaced by a generated lattice when the list is empty.

No retention metal, stated explicitly. An honest option rather than a missing capability: it produces the stone field alone, which is what a layout preview is. Reported in the compiled field's notes so it can never be mistaken for a failure to build metal.

One bead per lattice corner of each stone, individually — four solids per stone. Each is a real sphere fused into the host, embedded below the surface so the boolean produces genuine 3D overlap rather than a tangent touch.

One bead per lattice corner, shared by every stone touching it. Genuinely fewer solids, and each names the stones it serves, so 'shared' is a checkable statement about the topology rather than a label.
A small cylinder standing normal to the host surface at each corner. Normal to the SURFACE, not vertical, which is what makes it a prong on a curved shank rather than a pin through it.

A pavé composes onto a compiled family or an explicit arrangement rather than replacing it, so 'three-stone with a pavé shank' is one design. Same composition contract Sprint 25 established for the halo.

A pavé and a halo coexist in one design: both compose onto the same placement and both build real stones. PARTIAL because a pavé cannot target the HALO's own plane — a halo has no metal to hold beads — so the two are concentric neighbours rather than one structure. Nothing prevents a dense field and a halo ring from occupying the same radius; that overlap is reported as a geometric fact, not refused.

The stones' own volumes cut out of the host, reusing `setting/seat.py` — the module whose source is asserted never to fuse a stone shape. Deliberately NOT called a seat: it has no bearing shoulder and makes no claim that a stone would sit correctly in it.

A cell outside the host's declared extent is either clipped or the whole field is refused, by declared policy. A clipped field reports how many cells it lost, so a field that lost a third of its stones to an edge is visible rather than silently smaller.
The field carries its own GemIdentity and an explicit placement may override it, resolved through the real Sprint 21 registry. Semantic only, exactly as for a single stone: it never affects geometry.

A field's `stoneRef` may name a stone specification other than 'primary', and that reference is preserved and reported. It does not resolve, because JDL carries exactly one `stone` — so such a field produces no geometry and says so (JM-PAVE-004).

One field per design. A shank pavé AND a gallery pavé in one document needs a list of fields, each with its own host and retention, plus a rule for what happens where two fields meet. The single field is `pave`, not `paves`, so the limitation is visible in the schema rather than implied.
A field following a non-circular stone's own girdle outline needs the outline-offset walk Sprint 25 already recorded as absent for halos. The planar host offers concentric circles and says so.

Whether two pavé stones, or a pavé stone and a halo stone, physically overlap is a GEOMETRIC fact Geometry Inspection reports for every named component pair. What does not exist is a rule interpreting that overlap as a defect — that requires a professional minimum this project has no evidence for.

A minimum pavé spacing, a minimum bead diameter, a maximum stone density, a settable seat depth, or whether a field could be cut by a setter. Each needs sourced professional evidence this project does not have, so none exists — see the brief's own prohibition on inventing them.

A pave compiles into arrangement primitives and is COMPOSED onto whatever placement the design declares. There is no second placement engine: the lattice is expressed as explicit arrangement instances and the angular sequence of a full planar ring comes from arrangement/radial.py, the same function the resolver uses for a RADIAL pattern.

Two host surfaces resolve: BAND_OUTER (cylindrical) and HEAD_PLANE (planar). Both are derived from the same constants.py expressions the assembly uses, never picked out of a solid - a face index is not reproducible across kernel versions. Reserved targets: BAND_INNER, BAND_SIDE, CUSTOM_SURFACE, HALO_PLANE, PRONG_SURFACE, SETTING_SURFACE.

A pave stone follows the host surface normal, which required a real axis tilt on the arrangement transform (ADR-011). Verified by measuring the built solid's bounding box, not by trusting the field: at 90 degrees a stone's X and Z extents swap exactly and its volume is unchanged.

JM-PAVE-001..006: the host resolves, the field compiles through the real compiler, clipped cells are reported, references resolve, the pitch is checked for MATHEMATICAL consistency against the stones' own footprint, and the execution boundary plus the professional-review requirement are stated on every field.
Named with real reasons and no builder: CHANNEL, GRAIN, SHARED_PRONG, THREAD_SET. Each is refused by the model rather than substituted with a bead.

compilationHash: design identity plus the compiler, Forge rule-set, geometry generator, CadQuery and OpenCascade versions. Implemented in backend/jewelmind/compilation/. definitionHash is unchanged and carried separately. See ADR-012.

Six of the eight conceptual fingerprint fields are read from real installed versions and participate in compilationHash; the two remaining (a separate exporter version, the operating environment) do not exist as versioned things. One reader, in compilation/environment.py, so the cache key and the Golden fingerprint cannot disagree.

In-memory OrderedDict, capped at 20, LRU, cleared on restart, keyed on compilationHash so a compiler/rule-set/kernel change misses rather than serving stale geometry (ALCHEMIST-GOV-010 now enforced). PARTIAL because it is volatile: nothing survives a restart, by design.

GeometryPlan is not a materialized object. ALCHEMIST-GOV-004 describes it conditionally and materializing it requires an ADR. Compilation output travels on GeneratedModel's setting_result/arrangement_result/pave_result.

No database of any kind exists: no technology, no schema, no migrations, no ORM, no driver, no declared dependency. The absence is intentional for this phase and is asserted by backend/tests/test_persistence_boundary.py. No technology has been chosen and no ADR selects one; that decision is open.

The domain and CAD layers import no database or storage technology and perform no filesystem I/O outside the asset-store abstraction, so a future persistence layer can be added without touching them. Asserted over the real package tree by AST inspection, not by convention.

No repository, DAO or data-access layer exists, and none was created: an unused interface would be the speculative abstraction this phase deliberately avoided. The boundary is proven by test instead. Projects, versions and variants remain PLANNED (see history.project_versioning).

Every JDL/domain model round-trips through plain JSON with a stable definitionHash, including the optional arrangement/family/halo/pave blocks. Not a claim that persistence exists — a checked statement that nothing in the domain blocks it. GeneratedModel is deliberately NOT serializable: it holds kernel objects, and geometry is reproduced from the definition plus the compilation fingerprint.

No authentication, accounts, sessions, roles or project ownership exist, and no auth dependency is declared. commercial.auth_payments_marketplace is OUT_OF_SCOPE per README/CLAUDE.md; this row records the persistence-layer prerequisite rather than reopening that scope decision.

Asset storage is a Protocol (stone/importing.py::StoneAssetStore) with a single content-addressed filesystem implementation. No object storage exists. The interface was found sufficient and left unmodified; its resolve() returns a Path today, which a future non-filesystem implementation would have to satisfy.

Round prong (PRIMARY axis, PRONG family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. The pre-Sprint-23 straight cylinder and still the default for every prong setting. Count, diameter and height are parameters, so a four- and a six-prong setting are one mode rather than two.

Tapered prong (PRIMARY axis, PRONG family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. A cone frustum: full radius at the base, `prongTipRatio` of it at the tip. A software reference taper, not a measured claw profile.
Claw prong (PRIMARY axis, PRONG family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. A cylindrical shaft fused to a tapered head, so the taper is concentrated near the tip.

V prong (PRIMARY axis, PRONG family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. A cylinder with a V notch cut into its tip. The notch angle and depth are construction parameters; no claim is made that a stone tip would seat correctly in one.

Shared prong (PRIMARY axis, PRONG family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. A prong serving two or more stones, expressed through EXPLICIT prong positions carrying `servesStoneInstanceIds`. The prongs are real solids and the assignment is reported per component. What is NOT provided: derivation of the shared position from the two stones' own geometry, so whether a shared prong reaches both stones it names is a geometric fact for inspection rather than a guarantee. No interface authors explicit positions yet, which is why Studio, Designer and Conversation are PLANNED for this mode.

Full bezel (PRIMARY axis, BEZEL family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. The continuous wall built by offsetting the stone's own girdle outline. Unchanged from Sprint 19 and preserved byte-identically, which is why it remains the bezel default.

Partial bezel (PRIMARY axis, BEZEL family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. The full bezel's own wall with evenly spaced angular openings cut through it, so a partial bezel can never be a different wall from the full one it derives from. Legitimately several solids — n openings leave n arcs, joined through the head below — and that solid count is reported rather than repaired.

Linear channel (PRIMARY axis, CHANNEL family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. Two parallel walls with the stones between them, with optional end caps. Extents default to the stone's own measured box, so the single-stone case needs no parameters. Multi-stone by declaration: a longer run holds the arrangement's instances and records their ids, without computing a single placement.

Transverse bar (PRIMARY axis, BAR family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. Transverse bars across a run, with the stones between adjacent bars. One component carrying every bar, with each bar's own offset reported. Spacing and length default to the stone's own measured extents.

Flush / gypsy (PRIMARY axis, FLUSH family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. A solid collar offset from the stone's girdle outline with the stone's own solid cut out of it. Requires REFERENCE_SEAT relief, because without the cut the collar buries the stone — a geometric precondition, refused by the generator and reported by JM-SETTING-010. The rim must stay below the stone's measured crown height.

Opposed tension (PRIMARY axis, TENSION family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=REQUIRED. Two opposing supports with the stone between them, each reaching inward past the stone's edge so the seat relief leaves a real groove. The geometry is complete and the structural behaviour is NOT MODELLED: no force, no spring-back, no retention claim. Professional review is required before this geometry means anything functional.
Basket head (HEAD axis, HEAD family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. The pre-Sprint-23 hollow cylindrical wall, reproduced character-for-character and still the default.

Peg head (HEAD axis, HEAD family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. A basket wall on a narrower solid peg, joined by a conical flare. The flare is structural, not decorative: without it the peg never touches the bore and the head is two disconnected solids.

Martini head (HEAD axis, HEAD family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. A hollow conical wall, wide at the girdle and narrow at the base. A software reference silhouette; no commercial martini proportion is claimed.

Tulip head (HEAD axis, HEAD family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. A concave flare approximated by stacked cone frusta following a quadratic. Section count and curve are construction choices.

Open gallery head (HEAD axis, HEAD family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. The basket wall with evenly spaced windows pierced through it, cut from the basket's own solid. Windows span only the middle of the height so a continuous rim survives and the head stays one connected body. Deliberately not called azure.

Bead (RETENTION axis, RETENTION family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. One bead per lattice corner of each stone, individually. A hemisphere raised at the corner — named honestly as a sphere, because a real bead's shape depends on the graining tool and the hand.

Shared bead (RETENTION axis, RETENTION family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. One bead per lattice corner, shared by every stone touching it — genuinely fewer beads, which is the point of the technique. Anchors are derived in the surface's own parameters so neighbouring stones agree about where a corner is.

Micro prong (RETENTION axis, RETENTION family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. A small cylinder normal to the host surface at each corner, capped with a hemisphere, built individually per stone.

Shared micro prong (RETENTION axis, RETENTION family). settingGeometry=True, professionalReview=NOT_REQUIRED. A micro prong at each shared lattice corner, serving every stone that touches it. Sharing is a property of the ANCHOR SET, not of the solid, which is why this maps to the same builder as MICRO_PRONG — exactly as BEAD and SHARED_BEAD already do.
Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. A bar with a varying cross-section. Same construction gap as CHANNEL_TAPERED: it needs a swept or lofted profile per bar.

Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. A milled decorative edge. It is a surface texture applied along the wall's rim, and no texturing or knurling operation exists in the pipeline; approximating it with beads would be a different structure wearing the name.

Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. The generated bezel wall is already open at both ends, so an 'open-back' bezel is not a distinct solid here. A genuine open-back bezel differs by carrying a pierced seat rail the stone rests on, and no seat with a bearing shoulder exists (SETTINGV2-GOV-009).
Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. One wall shared between two adjacent channel rows. It requires two hosted rows resolved together, and one setting builds one channel.

Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. A channel whose clear width narrows along its run, for a graduated row. It needs a lofted wall pair rather than a pair of prisms, and a loft over a long shallow taper is not yet verifiable here.
Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. A milled rim around a flush-set stone. Same texturing gap as BEZEL_MILLGRAIN.

Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. Retention metal for a hidden halo's own stones. Sprint 25 recorded halo settingGeometry as false and it still is: the halo layer composes placements, and no builder holds a halo member. A mode here would have nothing to build.

Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. Azure/ajouré work is arbitrary decorative piercing, whose pattern is not expressible as parameters. HEAD_OPEN_GALLERY is the parametric subset that is — evenly spaced windows through the wall — and it is deliberately not called azure.

Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. A cathedral head is defined by how the SHANK rises to meet it, which is shank geometry rather than head geometry. It belongs to a Shank milestone, not to this taxonomy.
Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. Two stacked galleries need a second head instance per setting, which the one-head-per-setting contract does not express.

Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. Interwoven curved rails require a swept solid along a 3D spline. The current pipeline builds solids of revolution and lofts reliably; a swept trellis is not yet verifiable, so no builder exists.

Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. Prongs placed at the stone's own named anchors (tip, cleft, corners). The anchors exist in Stone System v2; a placement strategy that consumes them does not, so OUTLINE_CARDINAL remains the non-round default and a compass-point request would silently be an outline-cardinal layout.

Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. An arbitrary swept prong cross-section. EXPLICIT positions are the escape hatch for LAYOUT; an arbitrary profile is a different escape hatch and no builder accepts one.

Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. Bars between adjacent pavé stones. Same topology reason as RETENTION_CHANNEL: a bar sits at a cell MIDPOINT, not at a corner. BAR_TRANSVERSE is the PRIMARY family that builds bars.

Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. A continuous rail holding a pavé row. The pavé's retention anchors are LATTICE CORNERS — the points where cells meet — which is the right topology for a bead and the wrong one for a rail that runs the whole row. Channel setting exists as its own PRIMARY family instead, which is where a rail's extent is actually stated.

Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. A raised grain, as distinct from a bead. Its shape depends on the graining tool and the setter's hand; RETENTION_BEAD's sphere is the deterministic CAD reference for the volume a grain occupies, and a second id mapped to the same solid would imply a difference that is not there.

Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. A tension setting whose grip is derived from the metal's actual elastic response. That is an engineering calculation requiring material properties and a validated model, neither of which exists here. TENSION_OPPOSED builds the opposing supports and makes no structural claim (see its own capability row).

Reserved: no builder, and not a SettingModeId member. Decorative structure below the gallery, joining a head to a shank or to a second head. It needs multi-head or rail geometry, and RESERVED_SUPPORT_ELEMENTS already records that a rail joins two heads while one setting builds one.
